# Infrastructure as code and cloud security

- Make secure defaults explicit in code and reusable modules. Do not rely on console state, default provider behavior, or a resource name implying privacy.
- Keep secrets and sensitive outputs out of source, variable defaults, state outputs, user data, plan logs, and CI arguments. Use the approved secret service and mark unavoidable outputs sensitive.
- Treat state and plan artifacts as sensitive: use encrypted remote storage, access controls, locking, versioning, audit, and separation by environment.
- Grant IAM to a dedicated workload identity with the smallest actions/resources/conditions. Avoid `*`, broad pass-role/impersonation, long-lived access keys, and trust policies without exact principal/audience/subject conditions.
- Default network ingress/egress and storage/resource policies to private. Do not expose management, database, SSH/RDP, metrics, or control-plane ports to `0.0.0.0/0`/`::/0`.
- Enable encryption in transit and at rest with managed keys appropriate to classification; define key administrators/users separately and include rotation/recovery/deletion safeguards.
- Enable required audit, access, flow, and data-event logs with protected centralized retention. Do not log secret payloads or make log buckets publicly writable/readable.
- Pin providers, modules, actions, and images to trusted versions/digests and commit lockfiles. Verify third-party module provenance before granting it credentials during plan/apply.
- Protect destructive resources with retention/versioning/backups/deletion controls proportionate to impact. Test restore paths and avoid public snapshots.
- For serverless, use per-function roles, narrow triggers, authenticated endpoints, bounded concurrency/time/payload, safe temporary storage, and no secrets in environment output/logs.
- Preserve IaC security scanning and policy checks. Do not add blanket skip annotations; scope exceptions to a resource/control with rationale, owner, compensating control, and expiry.
